english: The children give the elders a deep New Year bow.
tip: 께 (kke) is the honorific 'to' – it replaces 에게 (ege) when the receiver deserves respect: 어른들께 (eoreundeulkke) = to the elders.

english: The New Year bow is offered respectfully as a full bow.
tip: 드리다 (deurida) is the humble 'give' aimed upward at elders – so the bow is offered: 정성껏 드려요 (jeongseongkkeot deuryeoyo). To a friend you'd 주다 (juda) instead.

english: After bowing, the children receive New Year money.
tip: The order is the ritual: 세배를 하고 (sebaereul hago = do the bow, and then) 세뱃돈을 받아요 (sebaetdoneul badayo) – the money only follows the bow, never before.

english: Grandmother gave me New Year money.
tip: 께서 (kkeseo) marks an honored subject; the verb takes 주셨어요 (jusyeosseoyo).

english: The kids are really happy to get their New Year money.
tip: You can't state others' feelings directly – 기쁘다 (gippeuda = glad) becomes 기뻐하다 (gippeohada = show gladness) for other people: 아이들이 기뻐해요 (aideuri gippeohaeyo).

target: 고향 가는 기차표가 벌써 다 팔렸어요.
english: The train tickets home are already all sold out.
tip: 팔리다 (pallida) = get sold – it's 팔다 (palda = sell) with -리- (-ri-) making it happen to the tickets: 다 팔렸어요 (da pallyeosseoyo) = all sold out.

english: The trip home took a full five hours.
tip: A number + -이나 (-ina) means 'that much?!': 다섯 시간이나 (daseot siganina) = a whole five hours. Drop it and the trip just took five hours, no eye-roll.

english: May you receive many blessings this new year.
tip: 새해 복 많이 받으세요 (saehae bok mani badeuseyo) = the set New Year greeting.

target: 송편을 예쁘게 빚으면 예쁜 아기를 낳는대요.
english: They say if you shape songpyeon prettily, you'll have a pretty baby.
tip: -대요 (-daeyo) reports a saying: 낳는대요 = they say one will have (a baby).

english: We set the table carefully with the year's new grain.
tip: 햇- (haet-) before a food means this year's first harvest: 햇곡식으로 (haetgoksigeuro) = with the new grain, 햇감자 (haetgamja) = new potatoes. One syllable marks freshness.

english: On Chuseok evening we look at the full moon.
tip: 보름달 (boreumdal) = the full moon; Chuseok falls on a full-moon night.

english: Parents' Day is May 8th.
tip: Dates always use Sino-Korean numbers: 오월 팔일 (owol paril) = May 8, literally 'five-month eight-day'. Native numbers like 다섯 (daseot) never touch dates.

english: We pin a carnation on our parents' chest.
tip: 달아 드려요 (dara deuryeoyo): -아/어 드리다 (deurida) turns an action into a humble favor for an elder – pin it on for them. With friends the ending is -아/어 주다 (juda).

english: I took my parents out and we had dinner.
tip: 모시다 (mosida) = to accompany an elder respectfully; 모시고 = escorting them.

english: It's a day to thank our teachers.
tip: 감사드리다 (gamsadeurida) = to give thanks, humbly, to someone above you.

english: The teacher smiled brightly.
tip: 웃으셨어요 (useusyeosseoyo) = smiled, with honorific -(으)시- for the teacher.

english: After graduating, we visit our teacher.
tip: 찾아뵈다 (chajaboeda) = to visit an elder respectfully.

english: On Teachers' Day I think of my old homeroom teacher.
tip: Remembering happens to you in Korean – 생각나요 (saenggangnayo) means the memory 'comes up' by itself. The old teacher surfaces in your mind; you're not the one doing the thinking.

english: In Korea we eat seaweed soup on birthdays.
tip: 미역국 (miyeokguk) = seaweed soup, eaten on birthdays and after childbirth.

english: Happy birthday, Minsu.
tip: 생일 축하해요 (saengil chukhahaeyo) is literally 'I congratulate your birthday' – 축하하다 (chukhahada) is a verb, so Korean congratulates the day rather than wishing it happy.

english: Hwangap is the sixtieth birthday.
tip: 환갑 (hwangap) marks 예순 살 (yesun sal), the 60th birthday – one full cycle of the traditional 60-year calendar, which is why it gets its own name and a big family celebration.

english: Every birthday I call my parents.
tip: -마다 (-mada) glues 'every' straight onto a noun: 생일마다 (saengil-mada) = every birthday. No separate word needed – the noun itself carries it.

english: At the doljanchi the baby does the doljabi.
tip: 돌잡이 (doljabi) = the baby grabs an object to foretell its future.

english: At the doljabi the baby grabbed the pencil.
tip: In 돌잡이 (doljabi) the grabbed object foretells the future: 연필 (yeonpil) = a scholar's path.

target: 아기가 첫돌을 맞아서 온 가족이 기뻐해요.
english: The whole family is glad the baby has reached its first birthday.
tip: Korean won't state someone else's feelings directly – 온 가족이 기뻐해요 (on gajogi gippeohaeyo) uses -어하다 (-eohada), 'shows happiness'. Plain 기뻐요 (gippeoyo) is only for your own joy.

english: I'm a little sad my friend is leaving.
tip: 떠나서 (tteonaseo) folds 'because' into the verb with -서 (-seo) – the reason comes first, the feeling last: friend-leaves-so, I'm-sad. English runs the opposite way.

english: I'm suddenly getting angry.
tip: 화가 나다 (hwaga nada) = to get angry; the anger 화 "comes up."

english: I'm envious of my friend.
tip: 친구가 부러워요 (chinguga bureowoyo) marks the friend with 가 (ga) as the subject – 부럽다 (bureopda) works like 'is enviable', so the envied person is the subject, not an object.

english: I get so nervous before a presentation.
tip: 긴장돼요 (ginjangdwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda), 'become' – nerves happen to you in Korean, not something you are. 되 (doe) + 어 (eo) fuses into the 돼 (dwae) you see here.

english: I'm very nervous because of the interview.
tip: 긴장돼요 (ginjangdwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda = become) – nerves are something that happens to you in Korean, not something you are.
